extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, trial lawyers, and examiners who interview witnesses and evaluate testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating witness reliability and eliciting memory in legal settings using psychological principles of attention, association, unconscious processes, and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-of-day effects on psychical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are systematic alterations in psychical processes with time of day (increase from morning to noon, drop until five o’clock, increase until nine in evening, sink by midnight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform daily patterns — much depends on the individual and the instant of examination. The only fairly uncontradicted fact is that noon to five in the afternoon is often unfavorable. Where possible, avoid trying important cases requiring special consideration during that period. Consider interviewee's habitual schedule (e.g., dinner time) when scheduling; expect individual variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the subconscious in legal procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious operations are undervalued; many complex habitual acts and intellectual processes occur without consciousness and can reveal habits and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that people perform many acts unconsciously (walking, greeting, mechanical skills). These unconscious actions can be diagnostic of familiar environments and habits. Use awareness of unconscious routines to interpret behavior and testimony, but also note limits: recently performed non-habitual acts may not be unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of unconscious action
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious performance is strongest for deeply habitual acts; newly performed or non-mechanical acts are less likely to be unconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting an unconscious action, distinguish between deeply practiced routines (very likely unconscious) and recently executed, one-off actions (likely conscious). Example: forgetting you prepared a cigarette is different from forgetting how to roll one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor sudden explanations as possible subconscious thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses later provide different, better explanations that 'suddenly occurred' to them, this may reflect genuine subconscious thinking rather than deliberate fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reflexively disbelieve a new probable exposition simply because it arose 'suddenly'—the brain registers and works over impressions unconsciously, awakening latent residues and leading to sudden insight. Treat such statements as potentially genuine; investigate whether conditions permitted subconscious processing (no opportunity to study case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention as limited psychic energy shared by conscious and unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious attention and unconscious activities compete for a limited psychic energy; interruptions draw off attention from both kinds of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptualize attention as finite units (e.g., 100 units). If something suddenly demands more attention, it will interrupt both unconscious fiddling and conscious tasks. Use this to approximate what an individual could do simultaneously and to understand interruptions during testimony or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective centrality (self-centered ideation)
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to center ideation on the self, interpreting events and remembering primarily what relates to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect witnesses to notice or recall details most relevant to themselves (e.g., looking for their name/photo). Use this to predict omissions/attentions in testimony. When evaluating descriptions, consider how the witness's self-reference shaped perception and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language usage reveals background and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner and frequency with which a witness uses words, and the richness of forms in particular domains, can indicate nature, character, and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe vocabulary distribution for diagnostic clues (e.g., many terms for a subject suggest familiarity). Use such linguistic cues when inferring witness background or specific expertise relevant to the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume omission equals non-occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness omits facts that seem important, do not immediately conclude they did not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, attempt to 'teach' the witness the relevant conditions and relationships until they become part of habitual mental machinery—sketch context, explain causal links, and elicit memory. This is difficult but effective; the skilled examiner can elicit far more accurate recollection by guided contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples sparingly and with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples aid understanding but require similarity, not equality; 'Omnis analogia claudicat'—analogy limps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on examples because they may mislead: degrees of similarity are unclear to listeners. Use examples only in extreme cases and make their limitations explicit. Beware that thinking in examples can supplant genuine reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of expectation on perception
rubrics_metrics.description: What an observer expects strongly shapes what they perceive; expectation causes selective attention and omission of competing events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple observers report different versions of the same event, consider differing expectations as a major cause. Anticipated stimuli (e.g., a creaking gate) will be noticed disproportionately; stronger, unrelated events may be overlooked. Factor expectation into credibility assessments and questioning strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner dialogue (I/You) reveals divided ego states
rubrics_metrics.description: When people report addressing themselves as 'You' in internal self-reproach or persuasion, it signals a division between practical and considering ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to reported inner dialogues—phrases like 'How could you have behaved so foolishly!' indicate that the practical ego was alien to the considering ego at that moment, which helps explain subjective conditions and contradictions in testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroification and attention-seeking motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individuals exaggerate or fabricate events to gain attention, fame, or discussion—called 'heroification'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify heroification by lack of other motives and the presence of exaggeration for effect (e.g., false rape accusations to be talked about). Examine intent and check for absence of alternative motives. Do not dismiss such testimony entirely, but be alert to its telltale signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four grounds of association of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Association is determined by (1) similarity, (2) contrast, (3) co-existence/simultaneity, and (4) succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these association principles to help witnesses recall: prompt by similarity, contrast, contemporaneous cues, or sequence. Be aware of differing theoretical emphases (Hume: similarity/contact/causality; Lipps: similarity and simultaneity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity as central to association (and limits of reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theorists argue simultaneity (images present together in mind) may be the principal ground of association; others reduce inner associations to external co-existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to elicit associations, consider simultaneous mental presence as key. Also be cautious: apparent associations may arise from incomplete chains (connecting A to C via B) producing false inferences. Assess completeness of associative chains before treating linked memories as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhibition of associations by 'funded' complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals may inhibit associations that are not implied in their 'funded' mental complexes, so expected associations may not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If associations seem absent, consider psychological inhibition rather than absence of connection. Employ indirect methods to introduce conditions into the complex that will permit the association to arise, though this can be difficult in non-pedagogical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of accessing idiosyncratic associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal, subjective associations depend on private experiences (home, travels, relations) which are often unknown to the examiner and hard to reconstruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits: without profound knowledge of the witness's life, many associative cues cannot be induced. Practical implication: use local/contextual cues (place of crime, contemporaneous events) which are more commonly shared, or focus on dates by linking to public events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical expression of associations as cautious clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical reactions (e.g., itching when hearing certain descriptions) may accompany associations and sometimes indicate concealed knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such physical signs as mere clues, not proof. Be careful: accurate description of wounds can cause nervous persons to react even if innocent. If the wound is not described and the accused nonetheless reaches for the correct spot, that may be a useful lead—but verify with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of occurrence for 'getting an idea' (useful modes of recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory/idea occurrence manifests as: (1) constructive occurrence (intentional association), (2) spontaneous occurrence (sudden idea), (3) accluding occurrence (long retention leading to emergence), and (4) retrospective occurrence (backward association).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive occurrence when deliberately guiding a witness (ask about enemies, servants, etc., to generate leads). Allow for spontaneous occurrences and treat them as possibly genuine subconscious associations. Use accluding techniques (longest possible calm retention/straining) particularly with more intelligent, patient witnesses to elicit hidden recollections. Retrospective occurrence (associating backwards) is harder to use with others but can aid self-recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and recollection are central to witness reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a witness can tell the truth depends critically on perception and memory; memory is complex and variously organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers must consider not only veracity but the capacity to recall (what was noticed, how long, which parts sank deeper). Overlooking memory literature is inexcusable for criminalists; examine and account for memory phenomena when evaluating testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ignorance about mechanisms of memory
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no unified theory of memory; many philosophical and psychological accounts exist and our empirical knowledge is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept scientific uncertainty about memory mechanics. Use empirical findings and practical techniques from the literature (Ebbinghaus, Münsterberg, Ribot, etc.) rather than relying on simplistic assumptions. Study recommended authors to build a practitioner's understanding.
